Chapter 1 Introduction 1.1 Purpose of this book Living Labs - defined as physical or virtual spaces that bring together multiple stakeholders to collaboratively tackle societal challenges, fostering co-creation and real-world testing of solutions (Hossain, Leminen, and Westerlund 2019) - have become increasingly popular in development-oriented agronomy. Living Landscapes are territories shaped by the interactions between environmental processes, food production, governance, markets, and human decision-making. However, we observe that codesign processes nurtured in Living Labs and Living Landscapes often favor local knowledge over academic knowledge and are rarely informed by systematically collected data and analysis of this data (Baudron 2024). While local knowledge is invaluable, relying exclusively on it can inadvertently limit the creativity and problem-solving potential of the codesign process (Asten et al. 2009). In practice, this can lead to innovations that reflect existing practices (e.g., manure management, intercropping, minimum tillage) rather than exploring novel solutions to the key bottlenecks in the systems under study. While place-based research yields rich, context-specific insights, it is inherently time- and resource-intensive, making it essential to assess the representativeness of the case study so that the outcomes of the participatory process can be effectively scaled to broader regions. We argue that researchers have a crucial role in generating, organizing, analyzing, and presenting data at every stage of the codesign process, from diagnostic and needs assessment, to prototyping, testing, and evaluation (Giller et al. 2008). Diagnostics and analytical tools from systems agronomy can help make challenges, opportunities, and trade-offs more explicit, supporting evidence-based decision making and enhancing the creativity of the codesign process. Furthermore, because such place-based codesign is deeply valuable yet time-intensive, we argue that researchers must systematically assess the representativeness of the study sites to determine the broader applicability of local insights and ensure that participatory outcomes can be effectively scaled. At the same time, data cannot simply be presented to Living Lab members in raw form. To be useful in codesign, data must be adapted to the audience, for example through visualizations, simplified tables, interactive tools, or role-playing exercises, while still allowing participants to draw their own conclusions. This approach aligns with the principles of discovery learning, where participants engage actively with information, explore patterns, and derive insights themselves, thereby improving understanding, ownership, and the quality of the codesign outcomes. Moreover, the participatory process should engage a diverse range of stakeholders, including policymakers, who require clear evidence on how representative the broader network of research sites is in order to support wider scaling and policy integration. One example of a process where academic knowledge is essential and cannot be substituted by local knowledge is de novo design — the creation of novel cropping or farming systems that break away from existing practices and explore new possibilities (Meynard, Dedieu, and Bos 2012). Data-driven and model-based approaches allow researchers to explore alternative designs systematically, which can then feed into the codesign process in Living Labs and Living Landscapes. This book presents a set of reproducible, data-driven workflows integrating KoBoToolBox with R. With the use of examples, the book provides clear, step-by-step guidance for researchers and practitioners on how data can be used to enrich codesign processes. The book was compiled using the bookdown package (Xie 2025), which enables the seamless integration of R code, analytical results, and narrative into a single, fully reproducible document. The reader may ask: ‘Why a whole book on workflows, when such workflows can nowadays be generated in no time by Artificial Intelligence?’ This is a valid question. However, what we want to share is not so much the workflows themselves, but rather a series of methods that we believe are central to systems agronomy. The code is written in a deliberately straightforward style, avoiding unnecessary use of functions, loops and other layers of abstraction, with the aim of making the underlying logic clear to the reader and allowing subsequent adaptation and refinement to specific case studies. The workflows should therefore be seen as building blocks that are easy to understand and adapt. We believe that the knowledge acquired by working through them will be invaluable in critically assessing, adapting and refining workflows generated with the help of AI. A pdf version of this book is also available here: https://agritrop.cirad.fr/620194/. 1.2 KoboToolBox and R For the workflows in this book to be usable by the largest number, our approach is based on two open-source softwares: KoboToolBox (https://www.kobotoolbox.org/) and R (https://www.r-project.org/) operated through R-Studio Desktop (https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/). We use these softwares because they are open-source, used by a large community of practice, and under constant development. Digital surveys (e.g., using KoboToolBox) are much faster than surveys using pen and paper, reduce errors (no transcription and error trapping during recording) and allow for the data to be immediately available right after it’s collected. Digital surveys also offer the possibility of associating geolocations and multimedia data. KoboToolBox is free and open access, and includes a free secured server, with summary analysis and mapping functions (a major advantage of KoboToolBox over alternatives, Figure 1.1). KoboToolBox offers a set of easy to use tools, but complex logics can be built with them. KoboToolBox produces sharable forms and is XLSForm compatible (XLSForm is a simple spreadsheet format for designing digital data-collection forms). Data collection can be done offline. Progress of data collection can be monitored without being on-site. KoboToolBox also provides a question library, and has a growing community of practice and online help. Figure 1.1: Screenshot of the mapping functions of the KoboToolBox server R is an open-source and free software environment (both a language and a program). As a program language software, it offers replicability and shareability (a major difference with ‘point-and-click’ softwares). R has a large online community, is probably one of the most powerful computer environment for data analysis currently available, and became very popular across many disciplines. Amongst other functions, R reads and writes files, manipulates and summarizes data, runs statistical tests and models, and produces well-designed publication-quality plots. The core functionalities of R are extended by hundreds of packages (and growing). R interacts with other softwares, and the size of datasets analyzed is only limited by the machine used. 1.3 Structure of this book This book provides a collection of XLSForms (input to KoboToolBox) and well-documented R scripts developed during the implementation of the CGIAR initiative ‘Transformational Agroecology across Food, Land, and Water Systems’ (https://www.cgiar.org/news-events/news/cgiars-agroecology-initiative-transforming-food-land-and-water-systems-across-the-global-south) and the CGIAR Multifunctional Landscape (MFL) science program (https://www.cgiar.org/cgiar-research-portfolio-2025-2030/multifunctional-landscapes), and that can be adapted to other contexts and projects (Figure 1.2). Figure 1.2: Proposed workflow to support the codesign process with data, using two open-source softwares: KoboToolBox and R As such, the book is structured around two introductory chapters to prepare the workflows: Learning KoboToolBox and R Spatial datasets Two chapters at plot-scale: - Managing on-farm experiments - Evaluation on-farm experiments Three chapters at farm-scale: - Baselining - Farm typologies - Ecological Network Analysis Two chapters at landscape-scale: - Spatial prediction of crop damage - Potential manure production under current land use And four chapters at regional scale: - Spatial recommendation domains - Crop eco-physiological suitability - Soil and climate representativeness of trials - Technology extrapolation domains References

Make the response mandatory. Add a validation criterion. Click on ‘Settings’ –> click on ‘Validation criteria’ (left part of the frame) –> make the criteria ‘Less than or equal to’ 100. Click on the lower ‘+’ sign –> click ‘Add question’ –> click ‘Select one’ –> replace ‘New question’ by ‘Did you grow maize during the last season?’ –> replace ‘Option 1’ by ‘Yes’ and ‘Option 2’ by ‘No’. Make the response mandatory. Click on the lower ‘+’ sign –> click ‘Add question’ –> click ‘Date’ –> replace ‘Enter a date’ by ‘Planting date’. Add a skip logic. Click on ‘Settings’ –> click on ‘Skip logic’ (left part of the frame) –> click on ‘Add a condition’ –> select ‘Did you grow maize during the last season?’ –> keep the logic ‘Yes’ Click on the lower ‘+’ sign –> click ‘Add question’ –> click ‘Ranking’ –> replace ‘New question’ by ‘Reason to grow maize’ –> add a second choice –> Make 3 items to be ranked: food, income, and feed. Add the same skip logic as for ‘Planting date’ (only if the response to ‘Did you grow maize during the last season?’ is ‘Yes’ Click on the lower ‘+’ sign –> click ‘Add question’ –> click ‘Point’ Click on the lower ‘+’ sign –> click ‘Add question’ –> click ‘Acknowledge’ –> replace ‘Acknowledge’ by ‘Do you agree to be part of this survey?’. Drag this question so it becomes the first question. Click ‘Save’ (top right corner) Preview the form (eye icon, top left corner) Close the form. And deploy the form (if you don’t see the function to deploy, retrieve the test form in ‘Drafts’) 2.1.2 Filling forms on your android device Follow the steps here: https://support.kobotoolbox.org/data_collection_kobocollect.html Use this URL: https://kc.kobotoolbox.org, your user name and your password Go to ‘Get a Blank Form’, and get the form ‘test’ Go to ‘Fill a Blank Form’, select your form, fill it up, and save 2.1.3 Visualizing and downloading the collected data on your computer Go to ‘Summary’. Check that your entry(ies) is(are) there. Go to ‘Data’. Inspect the data. Go to ‘Map’ (top left of the ‘Data’ tab, bottom of the menu) Go to ‘Download’ –> Click on ‘Export’ –> Click on ‘Download’ in the section ‘Exports’. You have your data ready for analysis! 2.1.4 Saving a PDF of your questionnaire to share with colleagues Click on form preview (eye icon, top left corner) Click on ‘Print’ Change ‘Destination’ into ‘Save as PDF’ 2.1.5 Working with an XLSForm Click on ‘Form’ –> Click on ‘More action’ (‘…’) –> Click on ‘Download XLS’. Take a moment to study the content of the tab ‘survey’ and the tab ‘choices’. The tab ‘survey’ contains all your questions (in the order they appear in your form). The tab ‘choices’ contains all the factorial choices for your questions ‘Select one’ Save the XLS Form as ‘test2.xls’ Change the list name for the question ‘Did you grow maize last season’ into ‘maize’, in both the ‘survey’ and the ‘choices’ tabs. Change the list name for the question ‘Reason to grow maize’ into ‘reason’, in both the ‘survey’ and the ‘choices’ tabs. In the ‘survey’ tab, make all the answers as ‘required’ (except for geopoint) by changing ‘false’ into ‘true’ In the ‘survey’ tab, column ‘name’, simplify variable names (be careful spaces are not allowed!) into: ‘Name’, ‘Age’, ‘Maize’, ‘Pdate’, ‘Reason’, ‘Reason_label’. Remember to make the same changes in the ‘relevant’ column (e.g., change ‘Did_you_grow_maize_during_the_’ to ‘Maize’) Create a question ‘Sex of the head of the household’ under the question ‘Name of the head of the household’. In the ‘survey’ tab, insert a row, enter ‘select_one sex’ in ‘type’, ‘Sex’ in ‘name’, ‘Sex of the head of the household’ in ‘label’, ‘true’ in ‘required’. Save Go on your KoBoToolbox account and click on ‘New’ Click on ‘Upload an XLSForm’ Upload the file you created ‘test2.xls’ Click on ‘Create project’ (keep the name ‘test2’) Preview the form. You can also go on ‘Edit’ (pencil icon) to see the changes that have been made to the form 2.1.6 Adding cascading questions Save ‘test2.xls’ as ‘test3.xls’. In the ‘survey’ tab, add three rows before the question ‘Name of the head of the household’ In the first row, enter ‘select_one country’ (as type), ‘Country’ (as name), ‘Country’ (as label), ‘true’ (in required). Be careful with the designation of the list_name (no capital C) and the designations of the name and the label (capital C). In the ‘choices’ tab, add two columns ‘Country’ and ‘Province’ (after label) Add 14 rows corresponding to the 2 countries (Zimbabwe, Zambia), the 4 provinces (Manicaland, Matebeleland, Southern, Northern) and the 8 districts (Chipinge, Nyanga, Hwange, Beitbridge, Mazabuka, Monze, Mbala, Senga). Enter the right list_name for each (country, province, district), names (with capital letters), and label (with capital letters). For Province names, enter the corresponding Country in the column ‘Country’ you created. For District names, enter the corresponding Province name in the column ‘Province’ you created. Save Go on your KoBoToolbox account and click on ‘New’ Click on ‘Upload an XLSForm’ Upload the file you created ‘test3.xls’ Click on ‘Create project’ (keep the name ‘test3’) Preview the form. You can also go on ‘Edit’ (pencil icon) to see the changes that have been made to the form 2.1.7 An example of survey Once you are familiar with the basics of KoboToolbox, you can analyse a more complex XLSForm. The XLSForm used to build the survey questionnaire in KoboToolBox for the baseline survey of the CGIAR Agroecology Initiave in Zimbabwe can be found here: https://github.com/FBaudron/book_standardized_workflows/blob/main/02-learning_kobo_r/BASELINE%20SURVEY%20TOOL.xlsx. The PDF of the questionnaire is also provided: https://github.com/FBaudron/book_standardized_workflows/blob/main/02-learning_kobo_r/BASELINE%20SURVEY%20TOOL.pdf. Feel free to adapt this XLSform to your own use. We will use a sample of the data generated from this questionnaire in the next chapter. 2.2 Resources to learn R To work with R (https://www.r-project.org/) on your own computer, you need to download the program and install it, and install R-Studio Desktop (https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/), which is a separate program that makes R easier to use. There are many free resources on the web to learn R: R for Beginners by Emmanuel Paradis (https://cran.r-project.org/doc/contrib/Paradis-rdebuts_en.pdf) R tutorial by Kelly Black (https://www.cyclismo.org/tutorial/R/) Introduction to R by Ross Ihaka (https://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/~ihaka/120/Notes/ch02.pdf) The Art of R Programming (https://nostarch.com/artofr.htm) YouTube Playlist (https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLOU2XLYxmsIK9qQfztXeybpHvru-TrqAP)

Chapter 3 Spatial datasets

Chapter 3 Spatial datasets This chapter introduces the spatial datasets used in the workflows and explains how they can be accessed and prepared for analysis, using the R package terra (Hijmans 2024). Many raw input datasets can be downloaded via the R package geodata (Hijmans et al. 2024). Others can be accessed here: https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fo/9k1tio0ct9egi6e8ji0mu/ABTRVDOxB3Kp6k4muyjGJHo?rlkey=8eh2zmb47i843p99xv1l5yw0m&st=2qt7snru&dl=0. A standalone R script containing the workflow is available here: https://github.com/FBaudron/book_standardized_workflows/blob/main/03-spatial_datasets/spatial_datasets.R. We first load geodata and terra. We also provide a path where final spatial datasets are saved. if (!require("geodata")) install.packages("geodata") if (!require("terra")) install.packages("terra") library(geodata) library(terra) path = "Data" 3.0.1 Shapefile of sub-Saharan Africa We create a shapefile of sub-Saharan Africa from country admin zones available from the gadm() function of geodata. We save and plot it. ssa = geodata::gadm(country = c("AGO", "BEN", "BWA", "BFA", "BDI", "CMR", "CPV", "CAF", "TCD", "COM", "COD", "COG", "CIV", "DJI", "GNQ", "ERI", "SWZ", "ETH", "GAB", "GMB", "GHA", "GIN", "GNB", "KEN", "LSO", "LBR", "MDG", "MWI", "MLI", "MRT", "MUS", "MOZ", "NAM", "NER", "NGA", "RWA", "STP", "SEN", "SYC", "SLE", "SOM", "ZAF", "SSD", "SDN", "TZA", "TGO", "UGA", "ZMB", "ZWE"), level = 0, path = path) writeVector(ssa, "Data/Spatial/Processed/ssa.shp", overwrite = TRUE) plot(ssa) 3.0.2 Rasters derived from SPAM We download a 5 rasters that were derived from the Spatial Production Allocation Model (SPAM) (IFPRI 2020) including (1) a raster of total cropland area per grid cell (ha per cell), (2) a cropland mask, (3) a raster of harvested maize area, (4) a raster of value of food crops, and (5) a raster of value of non-food crops. These rasters can be downloaded here: https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fo/9k1tio0ct9egi6e8ji0mu/ABTRVDOxB3Kp6k4muyjGJHo?rlkey=8eh2zmb47i843p99xv1l5yw0m&st=2qt7snru&dl=0. The raster of total cropland area per cell was calculated as the sum of the physical area of 46 crop specific rasyers, with missing values treated as zero during aggregation. Because the summed estimates could exceed the physical area of a grid cell, total cropland area was capped at the cell’s physical area. The proportion of each cell under cropland was then calculated, and cells with at least 1% cropland were retained to construct a cropland mask. The cropland mask was applied to the cropland area, as well as the 3 other rasters. Input data for the calculation of these rasters can be found here: https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/FSSKBW. cropmask = rast("Data/Spatial/Raw/cropmask.tif") plot(cropmask, main = "Cropland mask") plot(ssa, add = T) writeRaster(cropmask, "Data/Spatial/Processed/cropmask.tif", overwrite = TRUE) cropland = rast("Data/Spatial/Raw/cropland.tif") plot(cropland, main = "Cropland area per cell") plot(ssa, add = T) writeRaster(cropland, "Data/Spatial/Processed/cropland.tif", overwrite = TRUE) We harmonize the spatial resolution and grid alignment of the harvested maize area raster with those of the cropland mask using bilinear interpolation. This method estimates values for the new grid cells from neighbouring cells, making it suitable for continuous variables. We then crop the raster to the extent of the study area and apply the cropland mask, setting cells outside the mask to NA. This ensures that the resulting raster has the same spatial grid as the cropland mask and covers only the area retained for analysis. maize_area = rast("Data/Spatial/Raw/spam2017V2r1_SSA_H_MAIZ_A.tif") maize_area = resample(maize_area, cropmask, method = "bilinear") maize_area = crop(maize_area, cropmask) maize_area = mask(maize_area, cropmask) names(maize_area) = "maize_area" writeRaster(maize_area, "Data/Spatial/Processed/maize_area.tif", overwrite = TRUE) # Log-transformed maize area maize_area_log = log1p(maize_area) plot(maize_area_log, main = "Maize area per cell (log scale)") plot(ssa, add = T) For value of food crops, the following crops were considered: banana, barley, beans, cassava, chickpea, coconut, cowpea, groundnut, lentil, other cereals, other pulses, other roots and tubers, plantain, pearl millet, potato, rice, sesame, small millet, sorghum, soybean, sweet potato, temperate fruits, tropical fruits, vegetables, wheat and yams. Conversely, for value of non-food crops, the following crops were considered: Arabica coffee, Robusta coffee, cocoa, cotton, other fibre crops, oil palm, other oil crops, tea, sugarcane, sugarbeet, sunflower and rapeseed. We harmonize spatial resolution of both rasters with the cropland mask, and mask cells outside of the cropland mask. value_food_crops = rast("Data/Spatial/Raw/value_food_crops.tif") value_food_crops = resample(value_food_crops, cropmask, method = "sum") value_food_crops = crop(value_food_crops, cropmask) value_food_crops = mask(value_food_crops, cropmask) names(value_food_crops) = "value_food_crops" writeRaster(value_food_crops, "Data/Spatial/Processed/value_food_crops.tif", overwrite = TRUE) # Log-transformed value of food crops value_food_crops_log = log1p(value_food_crops) plot(value_food_crops_log, main = "Value of food crops per cell (log-scale)") plot(ssa, add = T) value_nonfood_crops = rast("Data/Spatial/Raw/value_nonfood_crops.tif") value_nonfood_crops = resample(value_nonfood_crops, cropmask, method = "sum") value_nonfood_crops = crop(value_nonfood_crops, cropmask) value_nonfood_crops = mask(value_nonfood_crops, cropmask) names(value_nonfood_crops) = "value_nonfood_crops" writeRaster(value_nonfood_crops, "Data/Spatial/Processed/value_nonfood_crops.tif", overwrite = TRUE) # Log-transformed value of non-food crops value_nonfood_crops_log = log1p(value_nonfood_crops) plot(value_nonfood_crops_log, main = "Value of non food crops per cell (log-scale)") plot(ssa, add = T) 3.0.3 Soil data We prepare the following rasters (harmonize spatial resolution with the cropland mask, and mask cells outside of the cropland mask) from input data available in geodata: sand content in the 0–30 cm soil layer; soil pH in the 0–30 cm soil layer; plant available water capacity. sand_05 = soil_af(var = "sand", depth = 5, path = path) sand_15 = soil_af(var = "sand", depth = 15, path = path) sand_30 = soil_af(var = "sand", depth = 30, path = path) # Align to analysis grid sand_05 = resample(sand_05, cropmask, method = "bilinear") sand_15 = resample(sand_15, cropmask, method = "bilinear") sand_30 = resample(sand_30, cropmask, method = "bilinear") # Crop soil data to cropmask sand_05 = crop(sand_05, cropmask) sand_05 = mask(sand_05, cropmask) sand_15 = crop(sand_15, cropmask) sand_15 = mask(sand_15, cropmask) sand_30 = crop(sand_30, cropmask) sand_30 = mask(sand_30, cropmask) sand = (sand_05 * 5 + sand_15 * 10 + sand_30 * 15)/(5 + 10 + 15) names(sand) = "sand" writeRaster(sand, "Data/Spatial/Processed/sand.tif", overwrite = TRUE) plot(sand, main = "Soil sand 0-30 cm") plot(ssa, add = T) ph_05 = soil_af(var = "pH", depth = 5, path = path) ph_15 = soil_af(var = "pH", depth = 15, path = path) ph_30 = soil_af(var = "pH", depth = 30, path = path) # Align to analysis grid ph_05 = resample(ph_05, cropmask, method = "bilinear") ph_15 = resample(ph_15, cropmask, method = "bilinear") ph_30 = resample(ph_30, cropmask, method = "bilinear") # Crop soil data to cropmask ph_05 = crop(ph_05, cropmask) ph_05 = mask(ph_05, cropmask) ph_15 = crop(ph_15, cropmask) ph_15 = mask(ph_15, cropmask) ph_30 = crop(ph_30, cropmask) ph_30 = mask(ph_30, cropmask) ph = -log10((10^-ph_05 * 5 + 10^-ph_15 * 10 + 10^-ph_30 * 15)/(5 + 10 + 15)) names(ph) = "ph" writeRaster(ph, "Data/Spatial/Processed/ph.tif", overwrite = TRUE) plot(ph, main = "Soil pH 0-30 cm") plot(ssa, add = T) pawc = soil_af_water("tawcpf23mm", "erzd", path = path) pawc = resample(pawc, cropmask, method = "bilinear") pawc = crop(pawc, cropmask) pawc = mask(pawc, cropmask) names(pawc) = "pawc" writeRaster(pawc, "Data/Spatial/Processed/pawc.tif", overwrite = TRUE) plot(pawc, main = "Plant available water capacity") plot(ssa, add = T) Total soil nitrogen is extracted from AfSIS. It can be downloaded here: https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/15egyyj6g5522nqf8172w/soil_grid_ntot.tiff?rlkey=wjzv9vinh6l48h0xj8ymz6z6w&st=n0dyuk9m&dl=0. We harmonize the spatial resolution of the raster with the cropland mask, and mask cells outside of the cropland mask. soil_n = rast("Data/Spatial/Raw/soil_grid_ntot.tiff") # Align to analysis grid soil_n = resample(soil_n, cropmask, method = "bilinear") # Crop soil data to cropmask soil_n = crop(soil_n, cropmask) soil_n = mask(soil_n, cropmask) names(soil_n) = "soil_n" writeRaster(soil_n, "Data/Spatial/Processed/soil_n.tif", overwrite = TRUE) # Log-transformed value of soil total N soil_n_log = log1p(soil_n) plot(soil_n_log, main = "Soil total N 0-20 cm (log-scale)") plot(ssa, add = T) 3.0.4 Climate data We prepare the following rasters (harmonize spatial resolution with the cropland mask, and mask cells outside of the cropland mask) from input data available in geodata: Mean annual average temperature; Mean annual precipitation. tavg = worldclim_global(var = "tavg", res = 5, path = path) tavg = resample(tavg, cropmask, method = "bilinear") tavg = crop(tavg, cropmask) tavg = mask(tavg, cropmask) tavg = mean(tavg) names(tavg) = "tavg" writeRaster(tavg, "Data/Spatial/Processed/tavg.tif", overwrite = TRUE) plot(tavg, main = "Mean annual temperature") plot(ssa, add = T) prec = worldclim_global(var = "prec", res = 5, path = path) prec = resample(prec, cropmask, method = "bilinear") prec = crop(prec, cropmask) prec = mask(prec, cropmask) prec = sum(prec) names(prec) = "prec" writeRaster(prec, "Data/Spatial/Processed/prec.tif", overwrite = TRUE) plot(prec, main = "Mean annual precipitation") plot(ssa, add = T) 3.0.5 Socio-economic data Rural population density is extracted from (Lloyd, Sorichetta, and Tatem 2017), and livestock density from (Gilbert 2012). Both rasters can be downloaded here: https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fo/9k1tio0ct9egi6e8ji0mu/ABTRVDOxB3Kp6k4muyjGJHo?rlkey=8eh2zmb47i843p99xv1l5yw0m&st=2qt7snru&dl=0. Livestock density is expressed in Tropical Livestock Units (TLU), which aggregate the biomass of different livestock species using the following conversion factors: cattle (0.7 TLU), pigs (0.2 TLU), sheep and goats (0.2 TLU), and poultry (0.001 TLU). Both rasters are converted from density to counts per pixel by multiplying pixel values by pixel area. Counts are then aggregated to match the spatial resolution of the cropland mask, and cells outside the cropland mask are excluded. # Load rural population density (people/km2) rural_population = rast("Data/Spatial/Raw/rural_population_5km_2020_ssa.tif") # Convert population density to population count per pixel rural_population_area = cellSize(rural_population, unit = "km") rural_population_count = rural_population * rural_population_area # Aggregate population counts to the cropmask resolution rural_population = resample(rural_population_count, cropmask, method = "sum") # Crop and mask to croplandrural_population = crop(rural_population, cropmask) rural_population = crop(rural_population, cropmask) rural_population = mask(rural_population, cropmask) names(rural_population) = "rural_population" writeRaster(rural_population, "Data/Spatial/Processed/rural_population.tif", overwrite = TRUE) # Log-transformed value of rural population rural_population_log = log1p(rural_population) plot(rural_population_log, main = "Rural population, 2020 (log-scale)") plot(ssa, add = TRUE) # Load TLU density (TLU/km2) tlu = rast("Data/Spatial/Raw/tlu.tiff") # Convert TLU density to TLU count per pixel tlu_area = cellSize(tlu, unit = "km") tlu_count = tlu * tlu_area # Aggregate TLU counts to the cropmask resolution tlu = resample(tlu_count, cropmask, method = "sum") # Crop and mask to cropland tlu = crop(tlu, cropmask) tlu = mask(tlu, cropmask) names(tlu) = "tlu" writeRaster(tlu, "Data/Spatial/Processed/tlu.tif", overwrite = TRUE) # Log-transformed value of Tropical Livestock Units tlu_log = log1p(tlu) plot(tlu_log, main = "Tropical livestock units (log-scale)") plot(ssa, add = TRUE) Travel time to cities is extracted from (Nelson et al. 2019), using data available in geodata travel_time = geodata::travel_time(to = "city", size = 6, up = TRUE, path = path) travel_time = resample(travel_time, cropmask, method = "bilinear") travel_time = crop(travel_time, cropmask) travel_time = mask(travel_time, cropmask) names(travel_time) = "travel_time" writeRaster(travel_time, "Data/Spatial/Processed/travel_time.tif", overwrite = TRUE) # Log-transformed value of travel time to cities travel_time_log = log1p(travel_time) plot(travel_time_log, main = "Travel time to cities of at least 50,000 inhabitants (log-scale)") plot(ssa, add = T) References

Chapter 4 Managing on-farm experiments 4.1 Generating QR codes 4.2 Integrating QR codes in KoboToolBox surveys

Chapter 4 Managing on-farm experiments This chapter presents a workflow for collecting and managing data from on-farm experiments using KoboToolBox and R, with QR codes to ensure reliable identification of farms, trials and treatments. The use of QR codes provides an efficient and reliable system for identifying farms/trials and plots/treatments during data collection in on-farm experiments. Each QR code encodes a unique identifier that corresponds to a farmer/experimental site or a specific plot/treatment. During field monitoring, these codes can be scanned directly in KoboToolbox, automatically filling in the correct ID in the data collection form. This approach minimizes transcription and labeling errors, ensures consistent tracking of repeated measurements, and facilitates seamless integration of field data with analytical workflows in R. In the CGIAR Agroecology initiative in Zimbabwe, each farmer hosting a trial received an ID card with a unique QR code. Before any data collection on a given farm/trial, the card was scanned to confirm the correct trial site and verify that the farmer was present. Each plot within a trial also had its own signboard displaying a QR code linked to its treatment, ensuring every observation was associated with the correct experimental condition. Figure 4.1: ID card with unique QR code received by each farmer hosting a trial in the CGIAR Agroecology initiative in Zimbabwe (left) and signage with a unique QR code for each plot/treatment in the corresponding trial 4.1 Generating QR codes We will now demonstrate how to generate unique QR codes for both farms/trials and plots/treatments using the R package baRcodeR (Wu and Colautti 2022). if (!require("baRcodeR")) install.packages("baRcodeR") library(baRcodeR) For demonstration and data protection compliance, we will use fictional farmer names that do not correspond to any real individuals. This ensures that no personal information is used while illustrating the workflow. set.seed(123) given = c("Tendai", "Fungai", "Tawanda", "Ropafadzo", "Tafadzwa", "Nyasha", "Chiedza", "Anesu", "Munyaradzi", "Chenai", "Kudzai", "Tariro", "Simba", "Rutendo", "Kudzanai", "Vimbai", "Tanaka", "Blessing", "Shamiso", "Rudo", "Kuda", "Tinashe", "Chipo", "Prosper", "Sekai", "Loveness", "Godfrey", "Mercy", "Brenna", "Nokutenda", "Sibusiso", "Vusumuzi", "Eliazar", "Palesa", "Tafara", "Mandla", "Zvikomborero", "Tanyaradzwa") surname = c("Mupfumi", "Chikwepa", "Mazarura", "Nyamadzawo", "Chikora", "Makarau", "Gwekwerere", "Mandizha", "Sibanda", "Gonye", "Mtsvera", "Ndlovu", "Moyo", "Ncube", "Mapfumo", "Chidavaenzi", "Mutsvangwa", "Dube", "Mashingaidze", "Nyamapfene", "Gunda", "Mungano", "Chikowore", "Matambanadzo", "Zimuto", "Mabhunu", "Chinyoka", "Chimanikire", "Chiriseri", "Gwanyanya", "Madziva", "Mapiravana", "Gwatidzo", "Chikore", "Mashingairi", "Chirwa", "Chinyamurindi") n = 25 fake_names = paste(sample(given, n, replace = TRUE), sample(surname, n, replace = TRUE)) fake_names [1] "Sibusiso Mapiravana" "Kudzanai Gwekwerere" "Rutendo Sibanda" [4] "Tawanda Gonye" "Zvikomborero Chikowore" "Rutendo Chinyoka" [7] "Sekai Gwekwerere" "Loveness Chinyoka" "Godfrey Mapiravana" [10] "Tafadzwa Zimuto" "Godfrey Chikore" "Mercy Chiriseri" [13] "Munyaradzi Chikora" "Brenna Mandizha" "Tafara Ndlovu" [16] "Anesu Moyo" "Loveness Dube" "Chiedza Gwatidzo" [19] "Munyaradzi Chinyoka" "Shamiso Zimuto" "Mandla Gunda" [22] "Rutendo Mapfumo" "Tanaka Mabhunu" "Tariro Madziva" [25] "Kudzanai Chidavaenzi" 4.1.1 Generating QR codes for farmers/trials We now generate a first set of QR codes corresponding to farmers or trials. Each QR code encodes one of the fictional farmer names. The create_PDF() function from baRcodeR generates a printable PDF containing all QR codes and their labels, which can later be laminated or used on ID cards in the field (as represented in Figure 5.1 above). create_PDF(Labels = fake_names, numcol = 2, numrow = 4, Fsz = 8, name = "farms_qrcodes") knitr::include_graphics("farms_qrcodes.pdf") Once the PDF is created, each farmer has an identification label that can be scanned during data collection. Scanning the QR code in KoboToolbox automatically retrieves the farmer’s unique ID, ensuring that all data collected belong to the correct individual/site. 4.1.2 Generating QR codes for plots/treatments We will now generate QR codes for every combination of farmer × treatment. Each farm typically hosts multiple treatments or plots. In this example, there are three treatments per trial: ‘conventional practice’ (CONV), ‘conservation agriculture’ (CA), and ‘push-pull’ (PPULL). The expand.grid() function creates all combinations, which are then concatenated into unique identifiers such as: ‘Tendai Mupfumi-CONV’, ‘Tendai Mupfumi-CA’, ‘Tendai Mupfumi-PPULL’, etc. Each of these labels corresponds to a unique plot within a farmer’s trial. l = expand.grid(FR = fake_names, TR = c("CONV", "CA", "PPULL")) l = paste(l$FR, l$TR, sep = "-") create_PDF(Labels = l, numcol = 2, numrow = 4, Fsz = 8, name = "plots_qrcodes") knitr::include_graphics("plots_qrcodes.pdf") The resulting PDF contains QR codes for all farmer × treatment combinations, which can be printed on plot signboards (as represented in Figure 5.1 above). During fieldwork, scanning the plot’s QR code ensures that measurements (e.g., crop establishement, assessment of pest damage, estimation of yield) are automatically attributed to the correct farm and treatment. 4.2 Integrating QR codes in KoboToolBox surveys QR codes can be easily integrated into KoboToolbox surveys to automatically record the identity of farms/trials and plots/treatments during data collection. This ensures that each observation is correctly linked to its corresponding farmer/trial and plot/treatment without manual typing or risk of mislabeling. As an example, consider the survey questionnaire used to monitor on-farm experiments under the CGIAR Agroecology Initiative in Zimbabwe. The corresponding XLSForm (used to build the questionnaire in KoboToolbox) is available here: https://github.com/FBaudron/book_standardized_workflows/blob/main/04-managing_on_farm_experiments/EXPERIMENT%20SURVEY%20TOOL.xlsx. A PDF version of the questionnaire is also provided: https://github.com/FBaudron/book_standardized_workflows/blob/main/04-managing_on_farm_experiments/EXPERIMENT%20SURVEY%20TOOL.pdf. You can adapt this survey questionnaire to your own use. In this questionnaire, several variables are of type ‘barcode’: ‘farmID’, ‘plotID_1’, ‘plotID_2’, and ‘plotID_3’ (each trial consists of three treatments arranged in three separate plots). The three treatments are: ‘conventional practice’ (CONV), ‘conservation agriculture’ (CA), and ‘push-pull’ (PPULL). Each of these variables corresponds to a question where the enumerator scans a QR code instead of typing an ID. The farmID is obtained by scanning the farmer’s ID card, while each plotID corresponds to the QR code placed on a specific plot signboard (Figure 5.1). In the Kobo form, the questions for the three plots are grouped between ‘begin_repeat’ and ‘end_repeat’ statements. This looping structure allows enumerators to enter repeated measurements (e.g., pest assessment in several points in each plot, typically 5, following a W-shaped sampling pattern) efficiently and consistently. 4.2.1 Data from KoboToolBox surveys that include QR codes Once data have been collected in KoboToolbox, they can be exported in Excel format for analysis in R. To illustrate this, you can download a sample dataset generated from the survey described above here: https://github.com/FBaudron/book_standardized_workflows/blob/main/04-managing_on_farm_experiments/EXPERIMENT%20SURVEY%20DATA.xlsx. This dataset was downloaded directly from KoboToolbox as an Excel file. It contain pest damage data collected on sorghum over one season in three different plots (corresponding to the different treatments described above). The file is made of four sheets: one main sheet with general information (e.g., farm ID, enumerator name, date), and three treatment sheets, each corresponding to pest assessment data in one of the three plots recorded through the ‘begin_repeat’/‘end_repeat’ structure in the questionnaire. A standalone R script containing the full workflow below is available at the following link: https://github.com/FBaudron/book_standardized_workflows/blob/main/04-managing_on_farm_experiments/managing_experiments.R. We load the necessary packages and import the data in R. if (!require("openxlsx")) install.packages("openxlsx") if (!require("tidyr")) install.packages("tidyr") if (!require("lmerTest")) install.packages("lmerTest") if (!require("performance")) install.packages("performance") if (!require("ggeffects")) install.packages("ggeffects") if (!require("sjPlot")) install.packages("sjPlot") if (!require("DHARMa")) install.packages("DHARMa") library(openxlsx) library(tidyr) library(lmerTest) library(performance) library(ggeffects) library(sjPlot) library(DHARMa) data = read.xlsx("EXPERIMENT SURVEY DATA.xlsx", sheet = 1) sc1 = read.xlsx("EXPERIMENT SURVEY DATA.xlsx", sheet = 2) sc2 = read.xlsx("EXPERIMENT SURVEY DATA.xlsx", sheet = 3) sc3 = read.xlsx("EXPERIMENT SURVEY DATA.xlsx", sheet = 4) Each plot’s QR code (scanned in the field) produces a text string such as ‘Tendai Mupfumi-CA’ or ‘Rudo Makarau-CONV’. These strings combine the farmer’s name and the treatment applied to that plot. To make the data easier to analyze, we split each plot ID column into two new columns: farmer - extracted from the first part of the QR code label - and a renamed column for the treatment in that plot (e.g., ‘1st plot’, ‘2nd plot’). Since the farmer’s name is already recorded via the farmID QR code at the beginning of the survey, we later drop the redundant farmer column from each plot section. This leaves a clean dataset with one row per trial, including the farmer ID and treatments for the three plots. We also retain the submission ID (’_index’) to be able to later merge this data with pest assessment data. data = separate(data = data, col = "Scan.the.QR.code.of.the.1st.plot", into = c("Farmer", "1st plot"), sep = "-") data = data[, c(3, 17, 5:7)] data = separate(data = data, col = "Scan.the.QR.code.of.the.2nd.plot", into = c("Farmer", "2nd plot"), sep = "-") data = data[, c(1:3, 5:6)] data = separate(data = data, col = "Scan.the.QR.code.of.the.3rd.plot", into = c("Farmer", "3rd plot"), sep = "-") data = data[, c(1:4, 6)] We split the main dataset into three separate datasets, one for each treatment. Each of these treatment-specific datasets contains three key fields: the farmer name, the treatment name, and the submission ID. Submission ID will allow merging with the repeated pest assessment data collected in KoboToolbox. For each treatment dataframe, we reorder the columns to place the submission ID first. We also remove columns that are not needed for analysis (e.g., submission date), keeping only the fields required for analysis. data1 = data[, c(1:3)] data2 = data[, c(1:2, 4)] data3 = data[, c(1:2, 5)] sc1 = sc1[, c(11, 1:8)] sc2 = sc2[, c(11, 1:8)] sc3 = sc3[, c(11, 1:8)] We merge each treatment dataset with its corresponding pest assessment data using the submission ID. In KoboToolbox exports, ’_index’ identifies the main submission, while ’_parent_index’ links repeated sections. This merge ensures that each plot’s pest assessment data aligns correctly with the corresponding farmer and treatment. After merging, we rename the plot columns to ‘Treatment’. We then combine the six treatment datasets into a single unified dataset. The submission ID is removed since it is no longer needed after merging. Selected columns are renamed to clearly reflect their contents, including the ‘Farmer’ column (captured from the QR code scanned at the start of the form) and various pest damage scores. data1 = merge(data1, sc1, by.x = "_index", by.y = "_parent_index", all.y = TRUE) data2 = merge(data2, sc2, by.x = "_index", by.y = "_parent_index", all.y = TRUE) data3 = merge(data3, sc3, by.x = "_index", by.y = "_parent_index", all.y = TRUE) names(data1)[3] = "Treatment" names(data2)[3] = "Treatment" names(data3)[3] = "Treatment" data = rbind(data1, data2, data3) data = data[, -c(1)] names(data)[c(1, 4:10)] = c("Farmer", "armmoured_cricket_leaf_damage", "armmoured_cricket_damage_score", "fall_armyworm_leaf_damage", "fall_armyworm_frass_whorl", "fall_armyworm_damage_score", "stalk_borer_leaf_damage", "stalk_borer_damage_score") 4.2.2 Running basic statistical models on the cleaned data Using the cleaned and merged dataset, we fit a mixed-effects model to analyze the severity of fall armyworm damage. We first set the levels of the variable Treatment to ensure that ‘CONV’ (conventional practice) is used as the reference category, since R orders factor levels alphabetically by default. We then fit a generalized linear mixed-effects model to explain the variability in fall armyworm severity scores. Treatment and crop growth stage (Vstage) are included as fixed effects, while the farm (Farmer) is included as a random effect to account for variability among farms. Because the severity score is discrete (1–9), we use a Poisson distribution. We evaluate model performance using the function check_model() of the R package performance (Lüdecke et al. 2021) to ensure the assumptions of the mixed-effects model are reasonably met. data$Treatment = factor(data$Treatment, levels = c("CONV", "CA", "PPULL")) mod_faw_severity = glmer(fall_armyworm_damage_score ~ Treatment + Vstage + (1 | Farmer), data = data, family = poisson()) check_plot = check_model(mod_faw_severity) print(check_plot) We examine the model results using both ANOVA and the model summary to assess the significance of fixed effects and to understand the estimated coefficients. anova(mod_faw_severity) Analysis of Variance Table npar Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Treatment 2 0.0169 0.0085 0.0085 Vstage 1 5.4042 5.4042 5.4042 summary(mod_faw_severity) Generalized linear mixed model fit by maximum likelihood (Laplace Approximation) [glmerMod] Family: poisson ( log ) Formula: fall_armyworm_damage_score ~ Treatment + Vstage + (1 | Farmer) Data: data AIC BIC logLik -2*log(L) df.resid 424.5 439.3 -207.2 414.5 138 Scaled residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -1.01490 -0.33144 -0.04122 0.28653 3.09858 Random effects: Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. This allows us to interpret the expected damage under different management practices. predict_response(mod_faw_severity, terms = "Treatment") # Predicted counts of fall_armyworm_damage_score Treatment | Predicted | 95% CI ---------------------------------- CONV | 1.98 | 1.19, 3.30 CA | 2.02 | 1.19, 3.44 PPULL | 2.01 | 1.21, 3.33 Adjusted for: * Vstage = 3.35 * Farmer = 0 (population-level) Finally, we visualize the predicted mean severity scores for each treatment, which helps to compare the expected pest damage across different treatments. plot_model(mod_faw_severity, type = "pred", pred.type = "fe", terms = "Treatment") References

Chapter 5 Evaluating on-farm experiments 5.1 Visualization of treatments’ performance 5.2 Shiny app

Chapter 5 Evaluating on-farm experiments This chapter presents a participatory approach to evaluating on-farm experiments, using visualization and interactive Shiny applications to explore results with farmers and other stakeholders. Building on a dataset covering two seasons (2022/23 and 2023/24) of on-farm trials on pest damage, crop yield, and farmers’ perceptions, we show how results can be explored interactively during field days, feedback meetings, or local workshops using Shiny applications. Shiny apps are interactive web applications built directly in R. They allow users to explore data dynamically — e.g., by selecting seasons or indicators — without requiring any programming knowledge. Because graphs and summaries update automatically when the user changes a selection, Shiny provides an intuitive interface for collective interpretation of results. These digital tools also enable farmers to see how their own fields contribute to wider patterns, creating a space where observations, interpretations, and preferences can be discussed openly. In this way, the Shiny app acts as a bridge between quantitative measurements and farmers’ qualitative, experiential knowledge, helping transform experimental results into practical insights for decision-making. Download the dataset used throughout this chapter here: https://github.com/FBaudron/book_standardized_workflows/blob/main/05-evaluating_on_farm_experiments/DATA%20FOR%20SHINY.xlsx. The data were collected on sorghum over two seasons and include pest incidence and severity, crop yield, and farmers’ overall evaluation of the three experimental treatments: conventional practice (CONV), conservation agriculture (CA), and push–pull (PPULL). The next code chunk loads the raw dataset, prepares factor variables, and separates the two seasons for later comparisons. A standalone R script containing the full workflow below is available at the following link: https://github.com/FBaudron/book_standardized_workflows/blob/main/05-evaluating_on_farm_experiments/visualization_of_treatments_performance.R. 5.1 Visualization of treatments’ performance Before introducing the interactive application, we build the graphs that will later be embedded in the Shiny interface, using data from the 2022/23 season (the app will allow the user to switch between this season and 2023/24). components: the user interface and the server logic. The user interface (ui) defines what participants see on the screen: dropdown menus (e.g., to choose a season), tabs to navigate between indicators, and the spaces where plots or tables will appear. It provides the visual structure of the app and determines how users interact with the data. The server component is where the analytical work takes place. It receives the user’s selections, filters or processes the data accordingly, performs calculations or summarisation, and generates the updated plots and tables that appear on the screen. Several R packages support this process. The core package is shiny (Chang et al. 2024), which provides the framework for building reactive web applications. Two additional packages improve the user experience of the app. bslib (Sievert, Cheng, and Aden-Buie 2025) allows customisation of the app’s appearance using Bootstrap themes, making the layout cleaner and compatible across devices. shinycssloaders (Attali and Sali 2024) adds animated loading indicators (‘spinners’) to plots so that users immediately see when a graph is being recalculated, which is helpful when working with larger datasets. What makes Shiny powerful is its use of reactive programming. Whenever a user changes a selection—choosing a different indicator or switching seasons—the app automatically re-runs only the parts of the code affected by that change and updates the outputs instantly. This creates the experience of a live, responsive system, even though all processing occurs within R. Thanks to this structure, Shiny apps can serve as accessible interfaces to complex datasets, allowing farmers and other stakeholders to explore results interactively and contribute to the interpretation. 5.2.2 Example of a Shiny app The Shiny script below reproduces the interactive application used in this chapter. It allows users to visualize the graphs developed above for a selected season and to explore three domains: pest damage, crop yield, and farmers’ perceptions. Chapter 7 Farm typologies 7.1 Concept of farm typology 7.2 Data preparation 7.3 Delineation of farm types 7.4 Interpretation of the farm typology 7.5 Selection of stratified samples

Chapter 7 Farm typologies This chapter presents a statistical approach to characterizing farm diversity and identifying representative farms for research and development activities. 7.1 Concept of farm typology Farm typologies aims at characterizing the diversity of farming systems and their distribution in heterogenous communities, as a basis for prioritizing interventions (Hammond et al. 2020) and/or to select representative farms, or ‘prototype farms’ (Alvarez et al. 2018). Various methodologies, all with their strengths and their weaknesses, are commonly used to delineate typologies, from (quantitative) statistical typology (Tittonell et al. 2010) to (qualitative) expert-based typology involving farmers and other knowledgeable stakeholders (B. Kebede 2009). Here, we use a statistical approach that combines Gower dissimilarities, principal coordinate analysis (PCoA), and partitioning around medoids (PAM). Gower dissimilarities allow continuous and categorical variables to be considered together when comparing farms. In the example below, we will use the small dataset we created in the previous chapter (and that was saved as a rds file). You can also download it here (and load it with the function read.csv()): https://github.com/FBaudron/book_standardized_workflows/blob/main/07-farm_typologies/small_dataset.csv A standalone R script containing the full workflow is available at the following link: https://github.com/FBaudron/book_standardized_workflows/blob/main/07-farm_typologies/farm_typologies.R. We first load the necessary packages. if (!require("openxlsx")) install.packages("openxlsx") if (!require("cluster")) install.packages("cluster") if (!require("gtsummary")) install.packages("gtsummary") if (!require("splitstackshape")) install.packages("splitstackshape") if (!require("randomForest")) install.packages("randomForest") library(openxlsx) library(cluster) library(gtsummary) library(splitstackshape) library(randomForest) 7.2 Data preparation We begin by importing the data. data = readRDS("small_dataset.rds") # data = read.xlsx('small_dataset.xlsx', sheet = 1) We first rename some variables, recode some categorical variables into binary ones, and convert NAs into zeros for some variables. names(data)[c(1, 4:6, 27, 29, 33:36)] = c("ID", "age_hhh", "sex_hhh", "edu_hhh", "cover_crops", "integrated_pest_management", "homemade_feeds", "fodder_production", "fodder_preservation", "survival_feeding") data$sex_hhh = as.numeric(data$sex_hhh == "Female") data$edu_hhh = as.numeric(data$edu_hhh != "Primary level") data$main_food_source = as.numeric(data$main_food_source == "Own production") data$main_income_source = as.numeric(data$main_income_source == "Crop sales" | data$main_income_source == "Livestock sales") data[c(23:36)][is.na(data[c(23:36)])] = 0 7.2.1 Removing outliers We remove extreme values to avoid skewing the analysis. For this, we plot and examine boxplots. Points beyond the whiskers of the boxplot have values higher than 1.5 times the interquartile range and are considered potential outliers. When such extreme points are observable, we remove them from the dataset. Age of the head of the household doesn’t have any true marked outlier. boxplot(data$age_hhh) But family size does. boxplot(data$family_size) Thus, we remove all records with a family size greater than 20. data = data[data$family_size < 20, ] boxplot(data$family_size) We inspect all other continuous variables, and find outliers for the number of small ruminants, the number of poultry, livestock offtake, and equipment value. We remove these extreme values from the dataset that we will use to delineate the farm typology. # boxplot(data$cropped_area) # boxplot(data$fallow) # boxplot(data$prop_non_cereals) # boxplot(data$fertilizers) # boxplot(data$amendment) # boxplot(data$cattle) # boxplot(data$small_rum) data = data[data$small_rum < 100, ] # boxplot(data$small_rum) # boxplot(data$poultry) data = data[data$poultry < 400, ] # boxplot(data$poultry) # boxplot(data$food_security) # boxplot(data$hdds) # boxplot(data$tot_div) # boxplot(data$cereal_prod) # boxplot(data$offtake) data = data[data$offtake < 6, ] # boxplot(data$offtake) # boxplot(data$eq_value) data = data[data$eq_value < 8000, ] # boxplot(data$eq_value) 7.2.2 Normalization of continuous variables To reduce the influence of extreme values, continuous variables are log-transformed. We create first a copy of the dataset before data transformation. typo = data We plot histograms of continuous variables, and when distribution departs too much from a Gaussian distribution, we logtransform the variable. In that case, we take care of adding a term - half of the minimum positive value - to avoid passing zeros to log10. Age of the head of the household has a relatively Gaussian distribution. hist(typo$age_hhh) But family size has a distribution that departs markedly from a Gaussian distribution. hist(typo$family_size) Thus, we logtransform the variable family size. typo$family_size = log10(typo$family_size + (0.5 * min(typo$family_size[typo$family_size > 0], na.rm = TRUE))) hist(typo$family_size) We inspect all other continuous variables, and find the total cropped area, the fallow area, the total quantity of fertilizer used, the total quantity of organic amendments used, the number of cattle, the number of small ruminants, the number of poulty, the total quantity of cereal produced, the livestock offtake, and the equipment value to depart markedly from a Gaussian distribution. We therefore log-transformed these variables. # hist(typo$cropped_area) typo$cropped_area = log10(typo$cropped_area + (0.5 * min(typo$cropped_area[typo$cropped_area > 0], na.rm = TRUE))) # hist(typo$cropped_area) # hist(typo$fallow) typo$fallow = log10(typo$fallow + (0.5 * min(typo$fallow[typo$fallow > 0], na.rm = TRUE))) # hist(typo$fallow) # hist(typo$prop_non_cereals) # hist(typo$fertilizers) typo$fertilizers = log10(typo$fertilizers + (0.5 * min(typo$fertilizers[typo$fertilizers > 0], na.rm = TRUE))) # hist(typo$fertilizers) # hist(typo$amendment) typo$amendment = log10(typo$amendment + (0.5 * min(typo$amendment[typo$amendment > 0], na.rm = TRUE))) # hist(typo$amendment) # hist(typo$cattle) typo$cattle = log10(typo$cattle + (0.5 * min(typo$cattle[typo$cattle > 0], na.rm = TRUE))) # hist(typo$cattle) # hist(typo$small_rum) typo$small_rum = log10(typo$small_rum + (0.5 * min(typo$small_rum[typo$small_rum > 0], na.rm = TRUE))) # hist(typo$small_rum) # hist(typo$poultry) typo$poultry = log10(typo$poultry + (0.5 * min(typo$poultry[typo$poultry > 0], na.rm = TRUE))) # hist(typo$poultry) # hist(typo$food_security) # hist(typo$hdds) # hist(typo$tot_div) # hist(typo$cereal_prod) typo$cereal_prod = log10(typo$cereal_prod + (0.5 * min(typo$cereal_prod[typo$cereal_prod > 0], na.rm = TRUE))) # hist(typo$cereal_prod) # hist(typo$offtake) typo$offtake = log10(typo$offtake + (0.5 * min(typo$offtake[typo$offtake > 0], na.rm = TRUE))) # hist(typo$offtake) # hist(typo$eq_value) typo$eq_value = log10(typo$eq_value + (0.5 * min(typo$eq_value[typo$eq_value > 0], na.rm = TRUE))) # hist(typo$eq_value) 7.3 Delineation of farm types We delineate farm types in three steps: (1) calculate a single Gower dissimilarity matrix combining continuous and categorical variables; (2) use principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) to represent the main dimensions of farm diversity; and (3) use partitioning around medoids (PAM) to identify groups of farms. 7.3.1 Preparing the typology dataset We first remove records with missing values in the variables used for the typology. This ensures that all farms are compared using the same set of variables and avoids pairwise differences in the information used to calculate dissimilarities. typo = na.omit(typo) 7.3.2 Calculating Gower dissimilarities We calculate dissimilarities among farms using the function daisy() from the R package cluster (Maechler et al. (2026)). We use Gower’s metric because the typology combines continuous variables with binary variables. Gower dissimilarity scales continuous variables according to their observed ranges and combines their contributions with those of categorical variables. The variables included are those previously used to describe the structural and functional characteristics of farms, together with the adoption of agricultural practices. Binary variables representing the presence or adoption of a characteristic are specified as asymmetric binary variables (asymm). This means that joint absences (two farms both lacking a characteristic) do not contribute to their similarity, whereas joint presences do. Household characteristics and the main sources of food and income are retained as symmetric binary variables. typology_vars <- c("age_hhh", "sex_hhh", "edu_hhh", "family_size", "cropped_area", "fallow", "prop_non_cereals", "fertilizers", "amendment", "cattle", "small_rum", "poultry", "food_security", "hdds", "tot_div", "cereal_prod", "offtake", "eq_value", "bee_hives", "ind_garden", "com_garden", "main_food_source", "main_income_source", "community_seed_banks", "small_grains", "crop_rotation", "intercropping", "cover_crops", "mulching", "integrated_pest_management", "compost_manure", "tree_planting_on_farm", "tree_retention_natural_regeneration_on_farm", "homemade_feeds", "fodder_production", "fodder_preservation", "survival_feeding") asymmetric_binary_vars <- c("bee_hives", "ind_garden", "com_garden", "community_seed_banks", "small_grains", "crop_rotation", "intercropping", "cover_crops", "mulching", "integrated_pest_management", "compost_manure", "tree_planting_on_farm", "tree_retention_natural_regeneration_on_farm", "homemade_feeds", "fodder_production", "fodder_preservation", "survival_feeding") diss <- cluster::daisy(typo[, typology_vars], metric = "gower", type = list(asymm = asymmetric_binary_vars)) 7.3.3 Reducing dimensionality using PCoA We use principal coordinate analysis (PCoA), implemented with cmdscale(), to represent the dissimilarities in a reduced number of dimensions. We retain the smallest number of axes accounting for at least 50% of the total variation represented by the eigenvalues. These axes are then used for clustering. pco <- cmdscale(diss, eig = TRUE, k = 10) # Inspect the eigenvalues barplot(pco$eig[1:20]) # Retain enough axes to account for at least 50% of the variation cum_var <- cumsum(pco$eig)/sum(pco$eig) k_axes <- which(cum_var >= 0.5)[1] k_axes [1] 3 pco_var <- pco$points[, 1:k_axes, drop = FALSE] 7.3.4 Selecting the number of farm types We use the average silhouette width to compare solutions with between 3 and 6 clusters. For each candidate number of clusters, we apply PAM to the Euclidean distances among farms in the retained PCoA space. The average silhouette width measures how well each farm fits within its assigned cluster compared with neighbouring clusters. We select the number of clusters with the highest average silhouette width. k_candidates <- 3:6 sil_width <- numeric(length(k_candidates)) names(sil_width) <- k_candidates for (k in k_candidates) { pam_fit <- cluster::pam(dist(pco_var), k = k, diss = TRUE) sil_width[as.character(k)] <- pam_fit$silinfo$avg.width } best_k <- as.integer(names(which.max(sil_width))) best_k [1] 3 plot(k_candidates, sil_width, type = "b", pch = 19, xlab = "Number of farm types", ylab = "Average silhouette width") abline(v = best_k, col = "red", lty = 2) 7.3.5 Classifying farms using PAM We run the final PAM classification using the retained PCoA axes and the selected number of clusters. PAM partitions farms around representative observations called medoids. Compared with methods based on cluster centroids, medoids are actual farms in the dataset and are therefore useful when identifying representative farms for subsequent analysis or on-farm research. final_pam <- cluster::pam(pco_var, k = best_k, diss = FALSE) grpPCO <- final_pam$clustering typo$type <- factor(grpPCO) # Add farm type to the original dataset data <- merge(data, typo[, c("ID", "type")], by = "ID") 7.3.6 Visualising farm types in PCoA space We plot the farm types on the first three PCoA axes to visualise how the groups are distributed in the reduced multidimensional space. plot(pco$points[, 1], pco$points[, 2], col = grpPCO, xlab = "PCO1", ylab = "PCO2") plot(pco$points[, 1], pco$points[, 3], col = grpPCO, xlab = "PCO1", ylab = "PCO3") plot(pco$points[, 2], pco$points[, 3], col = grpPCO, xlab = "PCO2", ylab = "PCO3") 7.4 Interpretation of the farm typology 7.4.1 Random forest To understand which variables are the most segregating in our typology, we fit a random forest classification model and assess variable importance through the Mean Decrease in Gini index using the R package randomForest (Liaw and Wiener 2002). The out-of-bag error rate and class-specific error rates provide an indication of how well the variables distinguish the farm types. These values are recalculated when the chapter is run and depend on the typology obtained from the PAM classification. data$type = as.factor(data$type) rf_type = randomForest(type ~ ., data = data[, -c(1:3)], ntree = 1500) print(rf_type) Call: randomForest(formula = type ~ ., data = data[, -c(1:3)], ntree = 1500) Type of random forest: classification Number of trees: 1500 No. of variables tried at each split: 6 OOB estimate of error rate: 9.73% Confusion matrix: 1 2 3 class.error 1 79 2 3 0.05952381 2 9 67 5 0.17283951 3 1 5 86 0.06521739 Next, we plot variable importance. The variable-importance plot identifies the variables that contribute most to distinguishing the farm types. Their relative importance is recalculated when the chapter is run. varImpPlot(rf_type) 7.4.2 Summary table To further interprete the typology, we produce a table from variables used in the delineation Chapter 8 Ecological Network Analysis This chapter uses ecological network analysis to characterize nitrogen flows and assess the functioning of diverse farming systems at the farm level. 8.1 Introduction Ecological Network Analysis (ENA) provides a framework to examine how nutrients circulate within farming systems. Farms with similar nutrient inputs or nutrient-use efficiency may nevertheless differ substantially in how nutrient flows are distributed among compartments and internal pathways, and in the extent to which nutrients are recycled and retained within the system. ENA allows these differences to be examined by representing the farm as a network of compartments (nodes) connected by directed, quantified flows, and analysing the properties that emerge from their joint organization (Rufino et al. 2009; Ulanowicz et al. 2009). Applied to mixed crop–livestock systems, ENA thus provides a way to move beyond the analysis of individual practices or nutrient-use efficiency towards an assessment of the functioning of the farming system as a whole This chapter presents an ENA of annual nitrogen flows at farm level (kg N per farm per year) to analyse the functioning of diverse farming systems in two districts of Zimbabwe (Mbire and Murehwa). The workflow combines farm-level nitrogen accounting, network analysis and comparisons across districts and farm types. Nitrogen is the currency used to quantify flows. The network comprises nine internal compartments representing crop, livestock, manure-management and household components of the farming system, and three additional boundary terms representing inputs entering the farm system, outputs leaving it, and dissipation. This representation allows us to characterize not only the magnitude of nitrogen flows, but also the cycling, integration and organization of the farm network. The diagram below summarizes the internal compartments, the system boundary and the main pathways considered in the analysis. It is a conceptual representation of the flow structure, the quantitative network is built separately for each farm. Figure 8.1: Conceptual representation of farms for the Ecological Network Analysis The nine internal compartments are as follows: Compartment Role in the network Important interpretation Cereals Aggregated cereal production Crop-specific details are aggregated into the cereal group. Legumes Aggregated legume production Retains the functional distinction between legumes and other crop groups. Garden crops Garden-crop production A production category, not a separate system boundary. Other crops Other crop production Crops not assigned to cereals, legumes or garden crops. Cattle Cattle production and associated feed, manure and product flows Kept separate from small ruminants to preserve pathway differences. Small ruminants Small-ruminant production and associated feed, manure and product flows Kept separate from cattle. Household Household use and transfers Household consumption is an internal transfer to this node, not automatically an export. Manure heap Manure collection, storage and processing Manure passes through this internal node before being returned to crop compartments. Fire Burning-related process represented in the current network Kept as a distinct node to represent the burning pathway in the farm N network. The three boundary terms are as follows: Input: nitrogen entering the farm system from managed and other external sources, together with explicitly identified accounting inputs. Output: nitrogen leaving the farm through recorded productive or other output pathways. Dissipation: nitrogen leaving internal compartments through recorded losses and residual dissipation added during accounting closure. The analysis has two complementary components. First, network indicators characterize the amount and organization of nitrogen moving through the farm system, including total system throughflow, path length, cycling and network overhead. Second, a functional flow budget groups flows according to their role in the farm system: managed external inputs, other boundary inputs, internal transfers and recycling, productive outputs, and other exports and losses. These functional categories are used to compare farms and explore associations with farm type and district. The analysis follows three steps: Balance farm nitrogen accounts. Recorded flows are assembled for each farm and internal compartment. Residual imbalances are identified and represented using explicit accounting adjustments, while keeping these adjustments distinct from measured flows. Run the ecological network analysis. A network is constructed for each farm, and indicators are calculated to describe nitrogen throughput, resource dependency, cycling and network structure. A complementary functional budget classifies flows according to their role in the farming system. Compare districts and farm types. Farm-level indicators and functional flow budgets are summarized and explored across the six district × farm-type groups. The example uses data from Murehwa and Mbire districts in Zimbabwe (farm_ena_flows_raw.xlsx), which can be downloaded here: https://github.com/FBaudron/book_standardized_workflows/blob/main/08-ecological_network_analysis/farm_ena_flows_raw.xlsx. A standalone R script containing the workflow is available here: https://github.com/FBaudron/book_standardized_workflows/blob/main/08-ecological_network_analysis/ecological_network_analysis.R. We first load the necessary packages. if (!require("tidyverse")) install.packages("tidyverse") if (!require("readxl")) install.packages("readxl") if (!require("enaR")) install.packages("enaR") if (!require("GGally")) install.packages("GGally") if (!require("ggplot2")) install.packages("ggplot2") if (!require("scales")) install.packages("scales") if (!require("gtsummary")) install.packages("gtsummary") library(tidyverse) library(readxl) library(enaR) library(GGally) library(ggplot2) library(scales) library(gtsummary) 8.2 Preparing and balancing farm nitrogen accounts 8.2.1 Preparing the data Load the survey-derived data from the following worksheets: farm_flows: farm-level directed flow records, including source, destination, nitrogen and dry matter quantities, and flow classification fields. ena_nodes: the names of the nine internal compartments. crop_production: crop-group area and production information used to calculate crop productivity indicators. ENA_to_Typology: links each ENA farm identifier to its district and farm type. It is an independent metadata input needed to stratify the pair plots; it is not an intermediate output of the ENA calculations. farm_flows = read_xlsx("Data\\farm_ena_flows_raw.xlsx", sheet = "farm_flows") %>% mutate(farm_id = as.character(farm_id), source = as.character(source), destination = as.character(destination), N_kg = as.numeric(N_kg), DM_kg = as.numeric(DM_kg)) ena_nodes = read_xlsx("Data\\farm_ena_flows_raw.xlsx", sheet = "ena_nodes") %>% pull(node) %>% as.character() crop_production = read_xlsx("Data\\farm_ena_flows_raw.xlsx", sheet = "crop_production") %>% mutate(farm_id = as.character(farm_id)) We separate internal transfers, boundary inputs, outputs and recorded dissipation. Nitrogen inflows and outflows are then summed for each farm × node. Existing survey-derived dissipation, including post-harvest losses and unused manure, is included before residuals are calculated, avoiding double counting. internal_flows = farm_flows %>% filter(source %in% ena_nodes, destination %in% ena_nodes) input_flows = farm_flows %>% filter(source == "Input", destination %in% ena_nodes) output_flows = farm_flows %>% filter(source %in% ena_nodes, destination == "Output") dissipation_flows = farm_flows %>% filter(source %in% ena_nodes, destination == "Dissipation") We then calculate the raw nitrogen balance for each farm × node. Recorded dissipation is included before any additional residual dissipation is calculated. node_balance_N = bind_rows(input_flows %>% group_by(farm_id, node = destination) %>% summarise(input_N = sum(N_kg, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop"), internal_flows %>% group_by(farm_id, node = destination) %>% summarise(internal_in_N = sum(N_kg, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop"), internal_flows %>% group_by(farm_id, node = source) %>% summarise(internal_out_N = sum(N_kg, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop"), output_flows %>% group_by(farm_id, node = source) %>% summarise(output_N = sum(N_kg, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop"), dissipation_flows %>% group_by(farm_id, node = source) %>% summarise(dissipation_N = sum(N_kg, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")) %>% group_by(farm_id, node) %>% summarise(input_N = sum(input_N, na.rm = TRUE), internal_in_N = sum(internal_in_N, na.rm = TRUE), internal_out_N = sum(internal_out_N, na.rm = TRUE), output_N = sum(output_N, na.rm = TRUE), dissipation_N = sum(dissipation_N, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>% right_join(tidyr::expand_grid(farm_id = sort(unique(farm_flows$farm_id)), node = ena_nodes), by = c("farm_id", "node")) %>% mutate(across(c(input_N, internal_in_N, internal_out_N, output_N, dissipation_N), ~replace_na(.x, 0)), balance_before_closure_N = input_N + internal_in_N - internal_out_N - output_N - dissipation_N) %>% arrange(farm_id, match(node, ena_nodes)) 8.2.2 Balancing farm nitrogen accounts The accounting closure is applied to each farm × compartment after all recorded inputs, internal transfers, outputs and dissipation have been included. A positive residual means that recorded inflows exceed recorded outflows; it is assigned to dissipation so that the compartment balance closes. A negative residual means that recorded outflows exceed recorded inflows and therefore requires a different interpretation. Crop deficits are represented by an Input → crop soil_N_input accounting flow, which makes the balance close but must not be interpreted as a measured soil-N flux. Livestock deficits are retained as livestock_N_balance_adjustment rather than being presented as genuine external inputs. Negative residuals in other compartments are not assigned an assumed pathway. Positive livestock residuals are labelled separately because they may include biomass retention as well as unmeasured losses. Crop deficits are represented as unmeasured soil-N inputs. This is an accounting term, not a measured soil-N flux. soil_N_input_flows = node_balance_N %>% filter(node %in% c("Cereals", "Legumes", "Garden_crops", "Other_crops"), balance_before_closure_N < -1e-10) %>% transmute(farm_id, source = "Input", destination = node, product = "soil_N", DM_kg = NA_real_, N_kg = -balance_before_closure_N, flow_type = "soil_N_input", mechanism = "unaccounted_soil_N") Negative residual in a livestock compartment is represented as a separate accounting adjustment, not as a measured external input. It is excluded from both real-input indicators below. livestock_balance_input_flows = node_balance_N %>% filter(node %in% c("Cattle", "Small_ruminants"), balance_before_closure_N < -1e-10) %>% transmute(farm_id, source = "Input", destination = node, product = "livestock_N_balance_adjustment", DM_kg = NA_real_, N_kg = -balance_before_closure_N, flow_type = "livestock_N_balance_adjustment", mechanism = "unmeasured_livestock_N_drawdown_or_missing_flow") Positive residuals are closed with an output to the Dissipation boundary.
