The trapezoidal membership function has four thresholds: the lower absolute limit, below which suitability is 0; the lower optimum limit, above which suitability increases to 1; the upper optimum limit, within which suitability remains 1; the upper absolute limit, beyond which suitability decreases to 0. Between the absolute and optimum limits, membership changes linearly. Thus, the fuzzy score is not a probability; it is a normalized representation of how closely a temperature value matches the specified suitability range. The thresholds used here are: Crop Absolute range (°C) Optimum range (°C) Maize 10–47 18–33 Sorghum 8–40 22–35 These values are the parameters adopted in this exercise from the crop-requirement information used to configure the script. Their suitability should be checked against the intended crop types and production environments before using the maps for decision-making. maize_main_temp_fuzzy = ifel(maize_main_tmean <= 10, 0, ifel(maize_main_tmean < 18, (maize_main_tmean - 10)/(18 - 10), ifel(maize_main_tmean <= 33, 1, ifel(maize_main_tmean < 47, (47 - maize_main_tmean)/(47 - 33), 0)))) maize_second_temp_fuzzy = ifel(maize_second_tmean <= 10, 0, ifel(maize_second_tmean < 18, (maize_second_tmean - 10)/(18 - 10), ifel(maize_second_tmean <= 33, 1, ifel(maize_second_tmean < 47, (47 - maize_second_tmean)/(47 - 33), 0)))) sorghum_main_temp_fuzzy = ifel(sorghum_main_tmean <= 8, 0, ifel(sorghum_main_tmean < 22, (sorghum_main_tmean - 8)/(22 - 8), ifel(sorghum_main_tmean <= 35, 1, ifel(sorghum_main_tmean < 40, (40 - sorghum_main_tmean)/(40 - 35), 0)))) sorghum_second_temp_fuzzy = ifel(sorghum_second_tmean <= 8, 0, ifel(sorghum_second_tmean < 22, (sorghum_second_tmean - 8)/(22 - 8), ifel(sorghum_second_tmean <= 35, 1, ifel(sorghum_second_tmean < 40, (40 - sorghum_second_tmean)/(40 - 35), 0)))) # Plot trapezoidal temperature suitability functions temp = seq(0, 50, by = 0.1) par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1)) # Maize maize_fuzzy = pmax(0, pmin(1, (temp - 10)/(18 - 10), (47 - temp)/(47 - 33))) plot(temp, maize_fuzzy, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "tomato", xlim = c(0, 50), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Mean temperature (°C)", ylab = "Suitability", main = "Maize") abline(v = c(10, 18, 33, 47), lty = c(2, 3, 3, 2), col = "grey50") # Sorghum sorghum_fuzzy = pmax(0, pmin(1, (temp - 8)/(22 - 8), (40 - temp)/(40 - 35))) plot(temp, sorghum_fuzzy, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "tomato", xlim = c(0, 50), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Mean temperature (°C)", ylab = "Suitability", main = "Sorghum") abline(v = c(8, 22, 35, 40), lty = c(2, 3, 3, 2), col = "grey50") par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) 12.3.2 Precipitation suitability Rainfall suitability is based on annual precipitation. The thresholds are: Crop Absolute range (mm/year) Optimum range (mm/year) Maize 400–1,800 600–1,200 Sorghum 300–700 400–600 The same trapezoidal logic is used: suitability increases linearly from the lower absolute limit to the lower optimum limit, remains at 1 within the optimum range, and decreases linearly to 0 between the upper optimum and upper absolute limits. Annual precipitation is a broad indicator. It does not account for the timing of rainfall, within-season dry spells, runoff, soil water-holding capacity or irrigation. These limitations are particularly relevant in semi-arid environments. maize_rain_fuzzy = ifel(prec_annual <= 400, 0, ifel(prec_annual < 600, (prec_annual - 400)/(600 - 400), ifel(prec_annual <= 1200, 1, ifel(prec_annual < 1800, (1800 - prec_annual)/(1800 - 1200), 0)))) sorghum_rain_fuzzy = ifel(prec_annual <= 300, 0, ifel(prec_annual < 400, (prec_annual - 300)/(400 - 300), ifel(prec_annual <= 600, 1, ifel(prec_annual < 700, (700 - prec_annual)/(700 - 600), 0)))) # Plot trapezoidal rainfall suitability functions prec = seq(0, 2000, by = 1) par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1)) # Maize maize_rain_curve = pmax(0, pmin(1, (prec - 400)/(600 - 400), (1800 - prec)/(1800 - 1200))) plot(prec, maize_rain_curve, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "tomato", xlim = c(0, 2000), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Annual precipitation (mm)", ylab = "Suitability", main = "Maize") abline(v = c(400, 600, 1200, 1800), lty = c(2, 3, 3, 2), col = "grey50") # Sorghum sorghum_rain_curve = pmax(0, pmin(1, (prec - 300)/(400 - 300), (700 - prec)/(700 - 600))) plot(prec, sorghum_rain_curve, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "tomato", xlim = c(0, 2000), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Annual precipitation (mm)", ylab = "Suitability", main = "Sorghum") abline(v = c(300, 400, 600, 700), lty = c(2, 3, 3, 2), col = "grey50") par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) 12.3.3 Soil pH suitability The soil pH thresholds are: Crop Absolute range Optimum range Maize 4.5–8.5 5.0–7.0 Sorghum 5.0–8.0 5.5–7.5 As with temperature and precipitation, the membership score ranges from 0 to 1. The thresholds describe a simplified response to soil pH and do not represent the full range of soil constraints that may affect crop growth. maize_ph_fuzzy = ifel(ph <= 4.5, 0, ifel(ph < 5, (ph - 4.5)/(5 - 4.5), ifel(ph <= 7, 1, ifel(ph < 8.5, (8.5 - ph)/(8.5 - 7), 0)))) sorghum_ph_fuzzy = ifel(ph <= 5, 0, ifel(ph < 5.5, (ph - 5)/(5.5 - 5), ifel(ph <= 7.5, 1, ifel(ph < 8, (8 - ph)/(8 - 7.5), 0)))) # Plot trapezoidal pH suitability functions ph_values = seq(3, 10, by = 0.01) par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1)) # Maize maize_ph_curve = pmax(0, pmin(1, (ph_values - 4.5)/(5 - 4.5), (8.5 - ph_values)/(8.5 - 7))) plot(ph_values, maize_ph_curve, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "tomato", xlim = c(3, 10), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Soil pH", ylab = "Suitability", main = "Maize") abline(v = c(4.5, 5, 7, 8.5), lty = c(2, 3, 3, 2), col = "grey50") # Sorghum sorghum_ph_curve = pmax(0, pmin(1, (ph_values - 5)/(5.5 - 5), (8 - ph_values)/(8 - 7.5))) plot(ph_values, sorghum_ph_curve, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "tomato", xlim = c(3, 10), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Soil pH", ylab = "Suitability", main = "Sorghum") abline(v = c(5, 5.5, 7.5, 8), lty = c(2, 3, 3, 2), col = "grey50") par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) 12.4 Combining suitability components 12.4.1 Maize For each maize season, the three fuzzy scores—temperature, precipitation and soil pH—are combined using an equal-weight arithmetic mean. na.rm = FALSE is used so that a final score is produced only where all three components are available. Chapter 13 Soil and climate representativeness of trials 13.1 Introduction 13.2 Preparing the data 13.3 Distribution of maize harvested area across climate and soil conditions 13.4 Representativity of the environmental classes covered by field sites

Chapter 13 Soil and climate representativeness of trials This chapter assesses the representativeness of field trials in terms of soil and climate conditions, by estimating the share of crop production environments covered by existing trial sites. 13.1 Introduction Field trials and demonstration plots are often implemented at a limited number of locations. Their findings are most readily extrapolated when the environmental conditions at these sites are representative of those under which the target crop is cultivated. This chapter assesses the environmental representativeness of existing trial sites across Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). The analysis characterises the climate and soil conditions associated with the harvested area of maize. It then locates field sites within these environmental distributions and estimates the share of maize harvested area occurring in environmental classes represented by at least one site. The approach is inspired by Figure 3 in Ruane et al. (2017). It focuses on four variables: mean annual temperature, annual precipitation, plant-available water capacity (PAWC), and total soil nitrogen. Climate and soil coverage are assessed separately. The resulting coverage measures are descriptive indicators of environmental representativeness. They do not assess representativeness in terms of management, farming systems, socioeconomic conditions, or environmental dimensions. Coverage also depends on the environmental variables selected and the classification scheme used, particularly the number and width of the classes. The workflow has three main stages: prepare the required data, including field-site locations; describe the distribution of maize harvested area across climate and soil conditions; assess the proportion of maize harvested area occurring in environmental classes represented by field sites. Here, the analysis is run for sub-Saharan Africa and maize. A standalone R script containing the workflow is available here: https://github.com/FBaudron/book_standardized_workflows/blob/main/13-soil_climate_representativeness/soil_climate_representativeness.R. We first load the necessary packages. if (!require("terra")) install.packages("terra") if (!require("geodata")) install.packages("geodata") if (!require("ggplot2")) install.packages("ggplot2") if (!require("dplyr")) install.packages("dplyr") if (!require("tidyr")) install.packages("tidyr") if (!require("knitr")) install.packages("knitr") library(terra) library(geodata) library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(knitr) library(dplyr) path = "Data" 13.2 Preparing the data 13.2.1 Environmental data and maize harvested area The shapefiles and rasters required for the analysis were produced in Chapter 3. They can also be downloaded here: https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fo/hdfjnxt05c7tyf2rkgm23/AMkKt6PRDyLops16iksFk68?rlkey=ppdlzleowakrd6apn666retvw&st=ul9fo7p3&dl=0. ssa = vect("Data/Spatial/Processed/ssa.shp") cropmask = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/cropmask.tif") mean_temperature = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/tavg.tif") annual_precipitation = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/prec.tif") soil_n = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/soil_n.tif") pawc = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/pawc.tif") environment_stack = c(mean_temperature, annual_precipitation, pawc, soil_n) names(environment_stack) = c("mean_temperature", "annual_precipitation", "pawc", "soil_n") We use the MapSPAM 2020 harvested-area raster for maize. The MapSPAM layer represents harvested area in hectares per source cell. The raster was produced in Chapter 3, but can also be downloaded here: https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/r9ws9nszvk9edxg24icmz/maize_area.tif?rlkey=iopz5i3jonq00io8xxrfjhsop&st=jw51gufc&dl=0. maize_harvested_area = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/maize_area.tif") global(maize_harvested_area, "sum", na.rm = TRUE) sum maize_area 35295543 13.2.2 Field-site locations The site table can be downloaded here: https://github.com/FBaudron/book_standardized_workflows/blob/main/13-soil_climate_representativeness/sites_Zim_Kenya_Combined.csv. It contains longitude and latitude in decimal degrees (WGS84). A codeSWstation column is used to identify sites in the figures. site_data = read.table("Data/sites_Zim_Kenya_Combined.csv", sep = ";", header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) sites = vect(site_data, geom = c("longitudeDD", "latitudeDD"), crs = "EPSG:4326") sites_cropmask = project(sites, crs(cropmask)) 13.3 Distribution of maize harvested area across climate and soil conditions 13.3.1 Mapping maize harvested area and field sites We map maize harvested area on the cropmask grid and the locations of the field sites. # Log-transformed maize area maize_harvested_area_log = log1p(maize_harvested_area) plot(maize_harvested_area_log, col = rev(hcl.colors(7, "YlOrRd")), main = "Maize harvested area (log scale) and field sites", plg = list(title = "Harvested area
(ha per cell)")) plot(ssa, add = T) plot(sites_cropmask, add = T, pch = 21, bg = "green", col = "black", cex = 1.5) 13.3.2 Classifying climate and soil conditions To compare the environmental conditions at field sites with those across the maize harvested area, each environmental variable is divided into 20 quantile-based intervals. The intervals are defined using the distribution of environmental values weighted by maize harvested area, so that each interval contains approximately 5% of the maize harvested area with valid data for the variable concerned. This approach gives greater resolution to environmental conditions that account for a large share of maize production, while avoiding the uneven representation that can arise when using equal-width intervals. The interval boundaries are estimated from a random sample of 50,000 cells within the maize-growing area, using harvested area as weights. For total soil nitrogen, quantiles are calculated on the logarithmic scale and then back-transformed to the original scale to account for its strongly skewed distribution. The same class boundaries are subsequently used to classify both the environmental rasters and the field-site locations. For each pair of variables, the same number of intervals is used on both axes. The heatmaps are plotted in class-index space, so that each tile has the same width and height even though the environmental variables have different units. Tile colour represents the share of maize harvested area in that combination of classes. # Restrict the range calculations to cells with maize harvested area maize_domain = ifel(maize_harvested_area > 0, 1, NA) temp_maize = mask(mean_temperature, maize_domain) rain_maize = mask(annual_precipitation, maize_domain) pawc_maize = mask(pawc, maize_domain) totn_maize = mask(soil_n, maize_domain) # Number of intervals (5% increments) n_intervals = 20 quantile_probs = seq(0, 1, length.out = n_intervals + 1) # Sample environmental values and harvested area from the same cells set.seed(123) environment_sample = terra::spatSample(c(temp_maize, rain_maize, pawc_maize, totn_maize, maize_harvested_area), size = 50000, method = "random", na.rm = TRUE, as.df = TRUE) names(environment_sample) = c("temperature", "rainfall", "pawc", "soil_n", "harvested_area") environment_sample = environment_sample |> filter(harvested_area > 0, soil_n > 0) # Calculate weighted quantiles weighted_quantile = function(x, w, probs) { ord = order(x) x = x[ord] w = w[ord] cumulative_weight = (cumsum(w) - 0.5 * w)/sum(w) approx(cumulative_weight, x, xout = probs, rule = 2)$y } temp_breaks = weighted_quantile(environment_sample$temperature, environment_sample$harvested_area, quantile_probs) rain_breaks = weighted_quantile(environment_sample$rainfall, environment_sample$harvested_area, quantile_probs) pawc_breaks = weighted_quantile(environment_sample$pawc, environment_sample$harvested_area, quantile_probs) # Calculate soil N quantiles on the log scale, then back-transform totn_breaks = exp(weighted_quantile(log(environment_sample$soil_n), environment_sample$harvested_area, quantile_probs)) # Ensure maximum values are included in the final interval temp_breaks[length(temp_breaks)] = temp_breaks[length(temp_breaks)] + 1e-08 rain_breaks[length(rain_breaks)] = rain_breaks[length(rain_breaks)] + 1e-08 pawc_breaks[length(pawc_breaks)] = pawc_breaks[length(pawc_breaks)] + 1e-08 totn_breaks[length(totn_breaks)] = totn_breaks[length(totn_breaks)] + 1e-08 # Classify the four environmental rasters temp_class = classify(mean_temperature, rcl = cbind(head(temp_breaks, -1), tail(temp_breaks, -1), seq_len(n_intervals)), right = FALSE) rain_class = classify(annual_precipitation, rcl = cbind(head(rain_breaks, -1), tail(rain_breaks, -1), seq_len(n_intervals)), right = FALSE) pawc_class = classify(pawc, rcl = cbind(head(pawc_breaks, -1), tail(pawc_breaks, -1), seq_len(n_intervals)), right = FALSE) totn_class = classify(soil_n, rcl = cbind(head(totn_breaks, -1), tail(totn_breaks, -1), seq_len(n_intervals)), right = FALSE) 13.3.3 Distribution across climate conditions We plot the climate envelope. # Number of classes for each variable n_temp <- length(temp_breaks) - Chapter 14 Technology extrapolation domains 14.1 Introduction 14.2 Preparing the data 14.3 Calculate technology transferability 14.4 Calculate cumulative reach 14.5 Calculate combined portfolio reach.

Chapter 14 Technology extrapolation domains This chapter presents a spatial approach to assessing the potential transferability of technologies from reference sites to other areas with similar environmental and socioeconomic characteristics. 14.1 Introduction Areas sharing similar farming system, environmental, and socio-economic characteristics with a given project site are assumed to have high potential for technology transfer, following the approach of Václavík et al. (2016). The underlying assumption is that technologies developed or tested in a particular context are more likely to be relevant in other areas with similar characteristics. Identifying such areas can help assess the potential geographical reach of research results and inform the scaling-up of agricultural technologies and innovations. In this example, we assess the transferability potential of technologies in the african Living Labs of the CGIAR Science Program on Multi-Functional Landscapes. The analysis uses a set of biophysical and socio-economic indicators to characterize the conditions surrounding each Living Lab and identify other cropland areas with similar characteristics. This chapter describes a spatial workflow for assessing the transferability of technologies from reference sites to other cropland areas. It combines environmental, soil, livestock, agricultural production and accessibility indicators to characterize the conditions surrounding each reference site. The similarity between each reference site and other cropland areas is quantified using Euclidean distances between their standardized indicator profiles. These distances are then converted into a transferability index, with higher values indicating greater similarity to the reference site. The workflow has three main stages: prepare and harmonize the spatial datasets; calculate a transferability index for each reference site; estimate the cumulative cropland and rural population potentially reached at different transferability thresholds. The final stage provides an indication of the potential geographical reach of technologies associated with each reference site. It allows the extent of potentially relevant cropland and the population living in these areas to be assessed at different levels of similarity. The transferability index is an indicator of similarity to the conditions of a reference site. It is not, by itself, evidence that a technology will perform equally well elsewhere. Agronomic validation remains necessary. A standalone R script containing the workflow is available here: https://github.com/FBaudron/book_standardized_workflows/blob/main/14-technology_extrapolation_domains/technology_extrapolation_domains.R. We first load the necessary packages. if (!require("terra")) install.packages("terra") if (!require("geodata")) install.packages("geodata") if (!require("sf")) install.packages("sf") if (!require("dplyr")) install.packages("dplyr") if (!require("ggplot2")) install.packages("ggplot2") if (!require("ggspatial")) install.packages("ggspatial") if (!require("tidyterra")) install.packages("tidyterra") library(terra) library(geodata) library(sf) library(dplyr) library(ggplot2) library(ggspatial) library(tidyterra) path = "Data" 14.2 Preparing the data Sections 14.2.1 and 14.2.2 are the same as sections 11.2.1 and 11.2.2 in Chapter 11. The shapefiles and rasters required for the analysis were produced in Chapter 3. They can also be downloaded here: https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fo/hdfjnxt05c7tyf2rkgm23/AMkKt6PRDyLops16iksFk68?rlkey=ppdlzleowakrd6apn666retvw&st=ul9fo7p3&dl=0. 14.2.1 Indicator stack ssa = vect("Data/Spatial/Processed/ssa.shp") cropland_fraction = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/cropland.tif") cropmask = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/cropmask.tif") sand = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/sand.tif") soil_n = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/soil_n.tif") awc = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/pawc.tif") mean_temperature = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/tavg.tif") annual_precipitation = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/prec.tif") tlu = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/tlu.tif") rural_population = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/rural_population.tif") value_food_crops = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/value_food_crops.tif") value_nonfood_crops = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/value_nonfood_crops.tif") travel_time = rast("Data/Spatial/Processed/travel_time.tif") indicator_stack = c(sand, soil_n, awc, mean_temperature, annual_precipitation, tlu, rural_population, value_food_crops, value_nonfood_crops, travel_time) names(indicator_stack) = c("sand", "soil_n", "awc", "mean_temperature", "annual_precipitation", "tlu", "rural_population", "value_food_crops", "value_nonfood_crops", "travel_time") plot(indicator_stack) 14.2.2 Transformation and standardisation of the data To reduce the influence of extreme values, we plot histograms of continuous variables, and when distribution departs too much from a Gaussian distribution, we log-transform the variable. In our case, soil_n, tlu, rural_population, value_food_crops, value_nonfood_crops, and travel_time have distributions that depart markedly from a Gaussian ones. terra::hist(indicator_stack, main = "Indicator distributions") We log-transform strongly right-skewed indicators, using log1p(), which handles zero values without requiring an arbitrary offset. We create first a copy of the raster stack before data transformation. indicator_transformed = indicator_stack vars_log = c("soil_n", "tlu", "rural_population", "value_food_crops", "value_nonfood_crops", "travel_time") for (v in vars_log) { indicator_transformed[[v]] = log1p(indicator_transformed[[v]]) } We inspect transformed variables to verify that the transformations behaved as expected. terra::hist(indicator_transformed, main = "Indicator distributions after transformation") The indicators are measured in different units and have different numerical ranges. They are therefore standardized using Z-scores before clustering. For each indicator \(k\), the standardized value is: \[ z_{pk} = \frac{x_{pk} - \mu_k}{\sigma_k} \] where \(x_{pk}\) is the value of indicator \(k\) in pixel \(p\), and \(\mu_k\) and \(\sigma_k\) are the mean and standard deviation of that indicator across the analysis domain. indicator_means = global(indicator_transformed, "mean", na.rm = TRUE) indicator_sds = global(indicator_transformed, "sd", na.rm = TRUE) indicator_means = as.numeric(indicator_means[, 1]) indicator_sds = as.numeric(indicator_sds[, 1]) indicator_z = (indicator_transformed - indicator_means)/indicator_sds names(indicator_z) = paste0(names(indicator_transformed), "_z") 14.2.3 Reference sites The reference sites are provided as a GeoPackage and can be downloaded here https://github.com/FBaudron/book_standardized_workflows/blob/main/14-technology_extrapolation_domains/ll_mfl.gpkg In this example, the layer contains polygons of the Living Labs in sub-Saharan Africa from the CGIAR Science Program Multi-Functional Landscapes, and a district attribute identifying each reference site. reference_sites = vect("Data/ll_mfl.gpkg") reference_sites = reference_sites[reference_sites$district %in% c("Senegal", "Ethiopia", "Kenya1", "Kenya2", "Zimbabwe", "Ivory Coast"), ] plot(ssa, main = "CGIAR MFL LL in sub-Saharan Africa") plot(reference_sites, add = TRUE, col = "blue") Each reference site is characterized by the mean value of each standardized indicator within its polygon. The resulting site profile represents the environmental and socioeconomic conditions associated with that site. The district attribute identifies the reference sites. site_names = unique(reference_sites$district) site_names = site_names[!is.na(site_names)] site_profiles = data.frame(site = site_names, matrix(NA_real_, nrow = length(site_names), ncol = nlyr(indicator_z))) names(site_profiles)[-1] = names(indicator_z) for (i in seq_along(site_names)) { site_polygon = reference_sites[reference_sites$district == site_names[i], ] # Dissolve polygons belonging to the same reference site site_polygon = terra::aggregate(site_polygon, by = "district", dissolve = TRUE) # Calculate the mean of each indicator within the site site_values = terra::extract(indicator_z, site_polygon, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE) site_profiles[i, -1] = as.numeric(site_values[1, -1]) } # Transpose site profiles: indicators in rows, reference sites in columns site_profiles_t = as.data.frame(t(site_profiles[, -1])) names(site_profiles_t) = site_profiles$site site_profiles_t = data.frame(Indicator = rownames(site_profiles_t), site_profiles_t, row.names = NULL, check.names = FALSE) site_profiles_t %>% knitr::kable(digits = 2, booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Mean standardized indicator values across reference sites") Table 14.1: Mean standardized indicator values across reference sites Indicator Senegal Ethiopia Kenya1 Kenya2 Zimbabwe Ivory Coast sand_z 0.93 -1.40 -1.44 -0.66 0.97 0.49 soil_n_z 0.07 1.72 1.70 0.53 -0.31 -0.18 awc_z -0.75 0.61 0.23 0.22 -0.26 0.57 mean_temperature_z 0.84 -0.91 -0.78 -1.08 -0.35 0.63 annual_precipitation_z -0.88 0.48 0.85 -0.59 -0.57 0.04 tlu_z 0.89 1.28 0.91 0.89 0.12 -0.10 rural_population_z 1.17 1.22 1.05 0.51 -0.27 0.20 value_food_crops_z 0.63 0.60 0.59 0.24 -0.84 0.43 value_nonfood_crops_z -0.18 0.86 1.16 0.13 0.29 1.06 travel_time_z -0.97 -0.79 -1.63 -0.63 0.09 -0.62 14.3 Calculate technology transferability For each reference site, the Euclidean distance between the site’s mean standardized profile and every cropland pixel is calculated. \[ d_{pi} = \sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^{K}(z_{pk}-\bar{z}_{ik})^2} \] where: \(d_{pi}\) is the distance between pixel \(p\) and reference site \(i\); \(z_{pk}\) is the standardized value of indicator \(k\) in pixel \(p\); \(\bar{z}_{ik}\) is the mean standardized value of indicator \(k\) at reference site \(i\); \(K\) is the number of indicators. Distance is converted into a transferability index using an exponential decay function: \[ Pr_{pi} = \exp(-\lambda d_{pi}) \] The parameter \(\lambda\) controls how rapidly transferability decreases as distance increases. A larger value produces a more restrictive transferability surface. The value used in the original script is 0.4. This parameter should be treated as an analytical choice and tested through sensitivity analysis. lambda = 0.4 transferability_stack = rast() for (i in seq_along(site_names)) { site_profile = as.numeric(site_profiles[i, -1]) distance_squared = (indicator_z - site_profile)^2 distance_to_site = sqrt(sum(distance_squared)) transferability = exp(-lambda * distance_to_site) names(transferability) = site_names[i] transferability_stack = c(transferability_stack, transferability) } The maps show the geographical distribution of pixels with different degrees of similarity to each reference site. plot(transferability_stack, range = c(0, 1), main = names(transferability_stack)) A transferability value close to one indicates high similarity to the reference site’s profile. A value close to zero indicates low similarity. 14.4 Calculate cumulative reach The cumulative reach analysis estimates the cropland area and rural population located in pixels with transferability values equal to or greater than a given threshold. The physical area of each pixel is calculated in hectares. Cropland fraction is then used to estimate the cropland area within each pixel. The following code accommodates cropland fractions expressed either as proportions or percentages. maximum_cropland_fraction = global(cropland_fraction, "max", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1] cropland_divisor = ifelse(maximum_cropland_fraction > 1, 100, 1) pixel_area_ha = cellSize(cropmask, unit = "ha") cropland_area_ha = pixel_area_ha * (cropland_fraction/cropland_divisor) cropland_area_ha = mask(cropland_area_ha, cropmask) The cumulative reach is calculated at thresholds from 1 to 0, in increments of 0.05. For each threshold, the cropland area and rural population in pixels meeting or exceeding the threshold are summed. transferability_thresholds = seq(1, 0, by = -0.05) total_cropland_ha = global(cropland_area_ha, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1] total_rural_population = global(rural_population, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1] Calculate cumulative reach for each reference site cumulative_reach = data.frame() for (i in seq_along(site_names)) { site_transferability = transferability_stack[[i]] cumulative_cropland = numeric(length(transferability_thresholds)) cumulative_population = numeric(length(transferability_thresholds)) for (j in seq_along(transferability_thresholds)) { threshold_mask = site_transferability >= transferability_thresholds[j] cumulative_cropland[j] = global(cropland_area_ha * threshold_mask, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1] cumulative_population[j] = global(rural_population * threshold_mask, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1] } site_reach = data.frame(reference_site = site_names[i], transferability_threshold = transferability_thresholds, cumulative_cropland_ha = cumulative_cropland, share_cropland_pct = 100 * cumulative_cropland/total_cropland_ha, cumulative_rural_population = cumulative_population, share_rural_population_pct = 100 * cumulative_population/total_rural_population) cumulative_reach = rbind(cumulative_reach, site_reach) } The cumulative reach curves show how the share of cropland and rural population increases as the transferability threshold becomes less restrictive. colour = reference_site)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + scale_x_reverse(breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.1)) + labs(x = "Transferability threshold", y = "Cumulative rural population share (%)", colour = "Reference site") + theme_bw() 14.5 Calculate combined portfolio reach. Individual transferability maps can overlap geographically. To calculate the combined reach of the portfolio, the maximum transferability value across all reference sites is calculated for each pixel. This creates an envelope representing the best match to at least one reference site. maximum_transferability = app(transferability_stack, fun = max, na.rm = TRUE) # Visual stretch: 1st–99th percentiles stretch_limits = quantile(terra::values(maximum_transferability), probs = c(0.05, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE) ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = maximum_transferability) + geom_spatvector(data = ssa, fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 0.3) + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", limits = stretch_limits, oob = scales::squish, name = "Transferability", na.value = "transparent") + coord_sf() + labs(title = "Maximum transferability across reference sites") + theme_bw() + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"), legend.position = "right", legend.title = element_text(size = 11), legend.text = element_text(size = 10), axis.title = element_blank(), panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA), plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)) + annotation_scale(location = "br", width_hint = 0.3) + annotation_north_arrow(location = "tl", which_north = "true", style = north_arrow_fancy_orienteering()) Below, we use a threshold of 0.6, but it can be changed depending on the desired level of similarity. selected_threshold = 0.6 combined_reach_mask = ifel(maximum_transferability >= selected_threshold, 1, NA) combined_cropland = mask(cropland_area_ha, combined_reach_mask) combined_population = mask(rural_population, combined_reach_mask) combined_cropland_ha = global(combined_cropland, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1] combined_rural_population = global(combined_population, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1] combined_reach_summary = data.frame(transferability_threshold = selected_threshold, unique_cropland_ha = combined_cropland_ha, share_cropland_pct = 100 * combined_cropland_ha/total_cropland_ha, unique_rural_population = combined_rural_population, share_rural_population_pct = 100 * combined_rural_population/total_rural_population) # Chapter 15 Conclusions

Chapter 15 Conclusions This book demonstrates that data can enrich every step of the codesign process, from the diagnostic stage, to the testing and validation stage, and the evaluation stage. Although related scripts have been presented sequentially, the process should be seen as iterative, rather than linear, as described for example in the DEED (Describe, Explain, Explore, Design) cycle (Giller et al. 2008; Falconnier et al. 2017). Negotiation is at the center of this process. The role of quantitative analysis (e.g., methods presented in this book) is to make on-going negotiations more explicit, creative and equitable. This implies a nonpartisan posture from researchers towards particular technologies and implies that the main function of living labs may be to serve as negotiation platforms (Moruzzo et al. 2024). We believe that some of the workflows presented in this new edition are also ensential to assist with site selection, understand the representativity and the transferability of the participatory, place-based research carried-out within various project. We hope this book can help scientists and practitioners make more use of data and data analysis in their codesign work. References
